title: Fisheries of the Exclusive Economic Zone Off Alaska; Pollock Fishing in the Winter Herring Savings Area of the Bering Sea and Aleutian Islands Management Area
summary:
Federal fisheries managers just announced two significant closures aimed at protecting fish stocks: the recreational season for greater amberjack in the Gulf of Mexico will close on September 27, 2025 and stay closed through July 31, 2026, and a key area of the Bering Sea is closing to pollock trawl fishing from September 25, 2025 to March 1, 2026 to limit herring caught by mistake. These decisions follow higher-than-allowed catches last season and are intended to help depleted populations recover.

In the Gulf, last year’s recreational catch of greater amberjack went far over the limit, which automatically triggers stricter measures the following year. Because of that overage, the allowed recreational catch for 2025–2026 is effectively zero, so the agency is closing the sector for the rest of the fishing year. During the closure, the bag and possession limit is zero in federal waters, and that also applies to federally permitted charter boats even when they are in state waters. Commercial amberjack harvest in the Gulf was already closed earlier this month after it surpassed its limit. In Alaska, the closure applies to the designated Winter Herring Savings Area in the Bering Sea. Regulators determined the herring bycatch allowance tied to the midwater pollock fishery has been reached, so they are temporarily stopping directed pollock trawling there, including by participants in community-based quota programs.

Who stands to benefit? In the short term, amberjack and herring get a breather, which supports healthier ecosystems and better fishing opportunities down the road. Protecting forage fish like herring can also help a wide range of marine life. In the longer term, rebuilding stocks can mean more stable seasons and income for fishing communities.

Who is likely to be hurt? Gulf recreational anglers, charter and headboat operators, bait and tackle shops, and coastal tourism businesses will feel the loss of an entire amberjack season. In the Bering Sea, pollock trawl vessels, community quota groups, processors, and associated supply chains may face reduced harvests and revenue while the closure is in effect. Some consumers could see tighter supply depending on how fleets adjust.

The National Marine Fisheries Service said it moved quickly, without the usual public comment period, to act on the latest data and avoid further harm to stocks that are already under rebuilding plans. The measures are temporary, but the impacts—good and bad—will be felt across the water and the waterfront.
